sentences.text: This quail-sized bird featured a long, tapering snout equipped with five pairs of small, conical teeth.
Its chest bone displayed unusual three-pronged projections on each side that looked like moose horns.
Feathers covered the body but were missing from the feet and the snout.
The longest primary feathers on the wings measured exactly 8 centimeters.
Like other enantiornitheans, it possessed a single pair of long feathers on its tail.
The genus was first described by Hou and colleagues in 2004.
Only one species, Longirostravis hani, is known within this genus.
Scientists know the animal from a single fossil specimen, IVPP V 11309, kept at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology.
Remains were discovered in the middle or upper Yixian Formation in Yixian County, China.
Researchers suggest the long snout was likely used for mud probing, similar to modern oystercatchers.
Longirostravis is classified within the extinct subclass Enantiornithes.
The genus belongs to the family Longipterygidae.
This extinct group of enantiornithean birds lived during the Early Cretaceous period, roughly 125 million years ago.
The species existed between the Barremian and Aptian stages, spanning from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
